saṃ. ni. 1.188, 250 “Ubhinnaṃ tikicchantaṃ taṃ, attano ca parassa ca;

Janā maññanti bāloti, ye dhammassa akovidā.

“When he is healing both—himself and the other—those who are unskilled in the Dhamma consider him a fool.

445.

445.

“Uppajje te sace kodho, āvajja kakacūpamaṃ;

Uppajje ce rase taṇhā, puttamaṃsūpamaṃ sara.

“If anger should arise in you, reflect on the Simile of the Saw. If craving for flavors should arise, remember the Simile of the Son’s Flesh.

446.

446.

“Sace dhāvati cittaṃ te, kāmesu ca bhavesu ca;

Khippaṃ [T 0.0335] niggaṇha satiyā, kiṭṭhādaṃ viya duppasu”nti;

“If your mind runs out to sensual pleasures and states of being, quickly restrain it with mindfulness, as one would a bad beast that eats the crops.”

… Brahmadatto thero….

… The Elder Brahmadatta…

13. Sirimaṇḍattheragāthā

13. The Verses of the Elder Sirimaṇḍa

447.

447.

udā. 45; cūḷava. 385; pari. 339 “Channamativassati[M 0.0289], vivaṭaṃ nātivassati;

Tasmā channaṃ vivaretha, evaṃ taṃ nātivassati.

The rain of offenses pours down on what is concealed; it does not pour down on what is revealed. Therefore, reveal what is concealed; thus, that rain will not pour down on it.

448.

448.

saṃ. ni. 1.66; netti. 18 “Maccunābbhahato loko, jarāya parivārito;

Taṇhāsallena otiṇṇo, icchādhūpāyito sadā.

The world is afflicted by death, surrounded by old age, pierced by the dart of craving, always smouldering with desire.

449.

449.

“Maccunābbhahato loko, parikkhitto jarāya ca;

Haññati niccamattāṇo, pattadaṇḍova takkaro.

The world is afflicted by death and enclosed by old age. Without a protector, it is always being struck, like a wrongdoer who has received his punishment.

450.

450.

“Āgacchantaggikhandhāva, maccu byādhi jarā tayo;

Paccuggantuṃ balaṃ natthi, javo natthi palāyituṃ.

Like approaching masses of fire are death, sickness, and old age. There is no strength to oppose them, no speed to flee from them.

451.

451.

“Amoghaṃ divasaṃ kayirā, appena bahukena vā;

Yaṃ yaṃ vijahate virahate (sī. pī.), vivahate (syā.) rattiṃ, tadūnaṃ tassa jīvitaṃ.

One should make the day fruitful, be it in a small or a large way; for with every night that passes, one’s life is diminished by that much.

452.

452.

“Carato tiṭṭhato vāpi, āsīnasayanassa vā;

Upeti carimā ratti, na te kālo pamajjitu”nti.

Whether one is walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, the final night approaches. This is no time for you to be heedless.

… Sirimaṇḍo sirimando (sī.) thero….

… The Elder Sirimaṇḍa…

14. Sabbakāmittheragāthā

14. The Verses of the Elder Sabbakāmi

453.

453.

“Dvipādakoyaṃ asuci, duggandho parihīrati pariharati (ka.);

Nānākuṇapaparipūro, vissavanto tato tato.

This two-footed body is impure, foul-smelling, and decaying, filled with various kinds of corpses, oozing from here and there.

454.

454.

“Migaṃ [V 0.0227] nilīnaṃ kūṭena, baḷiseneva ambujaṃ;

Vānaraṃ viya lepena, bādhayanti puthujjanaṃ.

As a hunter harms a hidden deer with a trap, a fish with a hook, or a monkey with glue, so do defilements afflict the worldling.

455.

455.

“Rūpā [T 0.0336] saddā rasā gandhā, phoṭṭhabbā ca manoramā;

Pañca kāmaguṇā ete, itthirūpasmi dissare.

Sights, sounds, tastes, smells, and delightful tangible objects—these five strands of sensual pleasure are found in a woman’s form.

456.

456.

“Ye [P 0.0048] etā upasevanti, rattacittā puthujjanā;

Vaḍḍhenti kaṭasiṃ ghoraṃ, ācinanti punabbhavaṃ.

Those worldlings with lustful minds who indulge in these increase the dreadful charnel ground; they accumulate renewed existence.

457.

457.

“Yo cetā parivajjeti, sappasseva padā siro;

Somaṃ visattikaṃ loke, sato samativattati.

But one who avoids these, as one would a serpent’s head with one’s foot, mindfully transcends this attachment in the world.

458.

458.

“Kāmesvādīnavaṃ [M 0.0290] disvā, nekkhammaṃ daṭṭhu khemato;

Nissaṭo sabbakāmehi, patto me āsavakkhayo”ti.

Having seen the danger in sensual pleasures and having seen renunciation as security, having escaped from all sensual pleasures, I have attained the destruction of the taints.

… Sabbakāmitthero….

… The Elder Sabbakāmi…

Chakkanipāto niṭṭhito.

The Book of the Sixes is finished.

Tatruddānaṃ –

The summary therein:

Uruveḷakassapo ca, thero tekicchakāri ca;

Mahānāgo ca kullo ca, mālukyo māluto (sī. ka.), māluṅkyo (syā.) sappadāsako.

Uruveḷakassapa, the Elder Tekicchakāri, Mahānāga, Kulla, Mālukya, and Sappadāsaka,

Kātiyāno migajālo, jento sumanasavhayo;

Nhātamuni brahmadatto, sirimaṇḍo sabbakāmī ca;

Gāthāyo caturāsīti, therā cettha catuddasāti.

Kātiyāna, Migajāla, Jenta, Sumana, Nhātamuni, Brahmadatta, Sirimaṇḍa, and Sabbakāmi; eighty-four verses, and fourteen elders are here.

7. Sattakanipāto

7. The Book of the Sevens

1. Sundarasamuddattheragāthā

1. The Verses of the Elder Sundarasamudda

459.

459.

“Alaṅkatā [T 0.0337][M 0.0291][V 0.0228][P 0.0049] suvasanā, māladhārī mālābhārī (sī.), mālabhārī (syā.) vibhūsitā;

Alattakakatāpādā, pādukāruyha vesikā.

Adorned, well-dressed, wearing garlands, embellished, with feet dyed with lac, the courtesan, having put on her sandals, stood there.

460.

460.

“Pādukā oruhitvāna, purato pañjalīkatā;

Sā maṃ saṇhena mudunā, mhitapubbaṃ mihitapubbaṃ (sī.) abhāsatha”.

Having taken off her sandals, her hands clasped in reverence before me, she spoke to me with soft and gentle words, smiling first.

461.

461.

“Yuvāsi tvaṃ pabbajito, tiṭṭhāhi mama sāsane;

Bhuñja mānusake kāme, ahaṃ vittaṃ dadāmi te;

Saccaṃ te paṭijānāmi, aggiṃ vā te harāmahaṃ.

‘You are young, one who has gone forth. Stay in my dispensation. Enjoy human sensual pleasures; I will give you wealth. Truly I promise you, or I will carry fire for you.’

462.

462.

“Yadā jiṇṇā bhavissāma, ubho daṇḍaparāyanā;

Ubhopi pabbajissāma, ubhayattha kaṭaggaho”.

‘When we become old, both of us leaning on staffs, we will both go forth, successful in both spheres.’

463.

463.

“Tañca disvāna yācantiṃ, vesikaṃ pañjalīkataṃ;

Alaṅkataṃ suvasanaṃ, maccupāsaṃva oḍḍitaṃ.

And having seen that imploring courtesan with hands clasped in reverence, adorned and well-dressed, it appeared like a snare of Death set out.

464.

464.

“Tato me manasīkāro…pe… nibbidā samatiṭṭhatha.

Then wise attention arose in me… and so on… revulsion became firmly established.

465.

465.

“Tato cittaṃ vimucci me…pe… kataṃ buddhassa sāsana”nti.

Then my mind was liberated… and so on… the Buddha’s teaching has been done.

… Sundarasamuddo thero….

… The Elder Sundarasamudda …

2. Lakuṇḍakabhaddiyattheragāthā

2. The Verses of the Elder Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya

466.

466.

Pare ambāṭakārāme, vanasaṇḍamhi bhaddiyo;

Samūlaṃ taṇhamabbuyha, tattha bhaddova jhāyati bhaddo’dhijhāyāyati (sī.), bhaddo jhiyāyati (syā. sī. aṭṭha.).

In the excellent Ambāṭaka Grove, in a forest thicket, Bhaddiya, having uprooted craving together with its root, that auspicious one meditates there.

467.

467.

“Ramanteke mudiṅgehi mutiṅgehi (sī. aṭṭha.), vīṇāhi paṇavehi ca;

Ahañca [T 0.0338] rukkhamūlasmiṃ, rato buddhassa sāsane.

“Some delight in kettle-drums, in lutes, and in small drums; but I, at the foot of a tree, delight in the teaching of the Buddha.”

468.

468.

“Buddho ce buddho ca (sabbattha) me varaṃ dajjā, so ca labbhetha me varo;

Gaṇhehaṃ sabbalokassa, niccaṃ kāyagataṃ satiṃ.

“If the Buddha were to grant me a boon, and if that boon could be obtained by me, I would accept for the entire world constant mindfulness directed to the body.”

469.

469.

“Ye [M 0.0292] maṃ rūpena pāmiṃsu, ye ca ghosena anvagū;

Chandarāgavasūpetā, na maṃ jānanti te janā.

“Those who judged me by my form, and those who followed me by my voice, being under the sway of sensual desire, those people do not know me.”

470.

470.

“Ajjhattañca [V 0.0229] na jānāti, bahiddhā ca na passati;

Samantāvaraṇo bālo, sa ve ghosena vuyhati.

“He does not know the internal and does not see the external. The fool, shrouded on all sides, is indeed carried away by the voice.”

471.

471.

“Ajjhattañca na jānāti, bahiddhā ca vipassati;

Bahiddhā phaladassāvī, sopi ghosena vuyhati.

“He does not know the internal but perceives the external. One who sees the fruit externally, he too is carried away by the voice.”

472.

472.

“Ajjhattañca pajānāti, bahiddhā ca vipassati;

Anāvaraṇadassāvī, na so ghosena vuyhatī”ti.

“But one who understands the internal and sees the external with insight, one who sees without obstruction, is not carried away by the voice.”

… Lakuṇḍakabhaddiyo thero….

… The Elder Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya …

3. Bhaddattheragāthā

3. The Verses of the Elder Bhadda

473.

473.

“Ekaputto [P 0.0050] ahaṃ āsiṃ, piyo mātu piyo pitu;

Bahūhi vatacariyāhi, laddho āyācanāhi ca.

“I was an only son, dear to my mother and dear to my father, obtained through many vows and entreaties.”

474.

474.

“Te ca maṃ anukampāya, atthakāmā hitesino;

Ubho pitā ca mātā ca, buddhassa upanāmayuṃ”.

“And they, out of compassion for me, desiring my welfare and seeking my good, both my father and my mother, led me to the Buddha.”

475.

475.

“Kicchā laddho ayaṃ putto, sukhumālo sukhedhito;

Imaṃ dadāma te nātha, jinassa paricārakaṃ”.

“‘This son was obtained with difficulty; he is delicate and has been raised in comfort. We give this little son to you, O Lord, as an attendant to the Victor.’”

476.

476.

“Satthā ca maṃ paṭiggayha, ānandaṃ etadabravi;

‘Pabbājehi imaṃ khippaṃ, hessatyājāniyo ayaṃ.

“The Teacher accepted me and said this to Ānanda: ‘Give this boy the going forth quickly; he will become a thoroughbred.’”

477.

477.

“Pabbājetvāna [T 0.0339] maṃ satthā, vihāraṃ pāvisī jino;

Anoggatasmiṃ sūriyasmiṃ, tato cittaṃ vimucci me.

“After the Teacher had me receive the going forth, the Victor entered his dwelling. Before the sun had set, thereupon my mind was liberated.”

478.

478.

“Tato satthā nirākatvā, paṭisallānavuṭṭhito;

‘Ehi bhaddā’ti maṃ āha, sā me āsūpasampadā.

“Then the Teacher, having risen from his seclusion, said to me, ‘Come, Bhadda!’ That was my higher ordination.”

479.

479.

“Jātiyā sattavassena, laddhā me upasampadā;

Tisso vijjā anuppattā, aho dhammasudhammatā”ti.

“At seven years of age by birth, I obtained the higher ordination. The three knowledges have been attained. Oh, the excellence of the Dhamma!”

… Bhaddo thero….

… The Elder Bhadda …

4. Sopākattheragāthā

4. The Verses of the Elder Sopāka

480.

480.

“Disvā [M 0.0293] pāsādachāyāyaṃ, caṅkamantaṃ naruttamaṃ;

Tattha naṃ upasaṅkamma, vandissaṃ vandisaṃ (sī. pī.) purisuttamaṃ.

“Having seen the best of men pacing in the shade of the mansion, I approached him there and paid homage to the supreme person.”

481.

481.

“Ekaṃsaṃ [V 0.0230] cīvaraṃ katvā, saṃharitvāna pāṇayo;

Anucaṅkamissaṃ virajaṃ, sabbasattānamuttamaṃ.

“Having arranged my robe over one shoulder and joined my hands in reverence, I followed him as he walked—the stainless one, the highest of all beings.”

482.

482.

“Tato pañhe apucchi maṃ, pañhānaṃ kovido vidū;

Acchambhī ca abhīto ca, byākāsiṃ satthuno ahaṃ.

“Then he questioned me, the wise one, the expert in questions. Unstartled and unafraid, I answered the Teacher.”

483.

483.

“Vissajjitesu pañhesu, anumodi tathāgato;

Bhikkhusaṅghaṃ viloketvā, imamatthaṃ abhāsatha”.

“When the questions had been answered, the Tathāgata approved. Having surveyed the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he spoke this matter:”

484.

484.

“Lābhā aṅgānaṃ magadhānaṃ, yesāyaṃ paribhuñjati;

Cīvaraṃ piṇḍapātañca, paccayaṃ sayanāsanaṃ;

Paccuṭṭhānañca sāmīciṃ, tesaṃ lābhā”ti cābravi.

“‘It is a gain for the people of Aṅga and Magadha, whose robe, almsfood, requisites, and lodging this one enjoys. Their welcoming and respectful service is a gain for them,’ he said.”

485.

485.

“Ajjatagge maṃ sopāka, dassanāyopasaṅkama;

Esā [T 0.0340] ceva te sopāka, bhavatu upasampadā”.

“‘From this day forth, Sopāka, you may come to see me. Let this itself, Sopāka, be your higher ordination.’”

486.

486.

“Jātiyā sattavassohaṃ, laddhāna upasampadaṃ;

Dhāremi antimaṃ dehaṃ, aho dhammasudhammatā”ti.

“Being seven years of age, having obtained the higher ordination, I bear my final body. Oh, the excellence of the Dhamma!”

… Sopāko thero….

… The Elder Sopāka …

5. Sarabhaṅgattheragāthā

5. The Verses of the Elder Sarabhaṅga

487.

487.

“Sare hatthehi bhañjitvā, katvāna kuṭimacchisaṃ;

Tena me sarabhaṅgoti, nāmaṃ sammutiyā ahu.

“Having broken reeds with my hands and made a hut, I lived; for that reason, my name became ‘Sarabhaṅga’ by convention.

488.

488.

“Na [P 0.0051] mayhaṃ kappate ajja, sare hatthehi bhañjituṃ;

Sikkhāpadā no paññattā, gotamena yasassinā.

“Today it is not allowable for me to break reeds with my hands; training rules have been laid down for us by the glorious Gotama.

489.

489.

“Sakalaṃ samattaṃ rogaṃ, sarabhaṅgo nāddasaṃ pubbe;

Soyaṃ rogo diṭṭho, vacanakarenātidevassa.

“Before, I, Sarabhaṅga, did not see the entire, complete disease. Now this disease is seen by me, who acts on the word of the supreme deva.

490.

490.

“Yeneva maggena gato vipassī, yeneva maggena sikhī ca vessabhū;

Kakusandhakoṇāgamano ca kassapo, tenañjasena agamāsi gotamo.

“By the very same path that Vipassī went, by which went Sikhī and Vessabhū, Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa, by that same straight path Gotama has gone.

491.

491.

“Vītataṇhā [M 0.0294] anādānā, satta buddhā khayogadhā;

Yehāyaṃ desito dhammo, dhammabhūtehi tādibhi.

“Devoid of craving, without grasping, the seven Buddhas have reached the state of exhaustion. By them, who have become Dhamma, the Such-like ones, this Dhamma was taught:

492.

492.

“Cattāri ariyasaccāni, anukampāya pāṇinaṃ;

Dukkhaṃ samudayo maggo, nirodho dukkhasaṅkhayo.

“The Four Noble Truths, out of compassion for beings: suffering, the origin, the path, and cessation, which is the exhaustion of suffering.

493.

493.

“Yasmiṃ [V 0.0231] nivattate yasmiṃ na nibbattate (ka.) dukkhaṃ, saṃsārasmiṃ anantakaṃ;

Bhedā [T 0.0341] imassa kāyassa, jīvitassa ca saṅkhayā;

Añño punabbhavo natthi, suvimuttomhi sabbadhī”ti.

“Wherein endless suffering in saṃsāra ceases; with the breakup of this body and the exhaustion of life, there is no further becoming. I am completely liberated from everything.”

… Sarabhaṅgo thero….

Thus the Elder Sarabhaṅga spoke these verses.

Sattakanipāto niṭṭhito.

The Book of Sevens is finished.

Tatruddānaṃ –

The summary:

Sundarasamuddo thero, thero lakuṇḍabhaddiyo;

Bhaddo thero ca sopāko, sarabhaṅgo mahāisi;

Sattake pañcakā therā, gāthāyo pañcatiṃsatīti.

The Elder Sundarasamudda, the Elder Lakuṇḍabhaddiya, the Elder Bhadda and Sopāka, and Sarabhaṅga the great seer: these five elders are in the Book of Sevens, with thirty-five verses.

8. Aṭṭhakanipāto

8. The Book of Eights

1. Mahākaccāyanattheragāthā

1. The Verses of the Elder Mahākaccāyana

494.

494.

“Kammaṃ [M 0.0295][V 0.0232][P 0.0052] bahukaṃ na kāraye, parivajjeyya janaṃ na uyyame;

So ussukko rasānugiddho, atthaṃ riñcati yo sukhādhivāho.

“One should not undertake much work; one should avoid company and not be enterprising. Eager and greedy for tastes, one forsakes the goal that is conducive to happiness.

495.

495.

“Paṅkoti hi naṃ avedayuṃ, yāyaṃ vandanapūjanā kulesu;

Sukhumaṃ sallaṃ durubbahaṃ, sakkāro kāpurisena dujjaho.

“Indeed, they have declared it a mire, this homage and veneration in families. A subtle dart, difficult to extract, honor is hard for a base man to relinquish.

496.

496.

“Na parassupanidhāya, kammaṃ maccassa pāpakaṃ;

Attanā taṃ na seveyya, kammabandhūhi mātiyā.

“A mortal should not do an evil deed on account of another, nor should one engage in it oneself; for beings have kamma as their kin.

497.

497.

“Na pare vacanā coro, na pare vacanā muni;

Attā ca naṃ yathāvedi yathā vetti (sī.), devāpi naṃ tathā vidū.

“Not by another’s word is one a thief; not by another’s word is one a sage. As one’s own self knows one, so too the gods know one.

498.

498.

“Pare ca na vijānanti, mayamettha yamāmase;

Ye [T 0.0342] ca tattha vijānanti, tato sammanti medhagā.

“Others do not realize that here we are heading to death; but those who do realize this, thereby their quarrels are stilled.

499.

499.

“Jīvate vāpi sappañño, api vittaparikkhayo;

Paññāya ca alābhena abhāvena (sī. aṭṭha.), vittavāpi na jīvati.

“A wise person lives on, even when his wealth is destroyed; but through lack of wisdom, even a wealthy person does not truly live.

500.

500.

“Sabbaṃ suṇāti sotena, sabbaṃ passati cakkhunā;

Na ca diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ dhīro, sabbaṃ ujjhitumarahati.

“One hears everything with the ear, one sees everything with the eye; but a wise person ought not to reject everything seen and heard.

501.

501.

“Cakkhumāssa yathā andho, sotavā badhiro yathā;

Paññavāssa yathā mūgo, balavā dubbaloriva;

Atha atthe samuppanne, sayetha passetha (ka.) matasāyika”nti.

“One with eyes should be as if blind, one with ears as if deaf, one with wisdom as if mute, one who is strong as if weak. Then when a matter of substance has arisen, one should lie down as if dead.”

… Mahākaccāyano thero….

Thus the Elder Mahākaccāyana spoke these verses.

2. Sirimittattheragāthā

2. The Verses of the Elder Sirimitta

502.

502.

“Akkodhanonupanāhī, amāyo rittapesuṇo;

Sa ve tādisako bhikkhu, evaṃ pecca na socati.

“A bhikkhu who is not prone to anger, not resentful, free from deceit, and devoid of slander; truly, such a bhikkhu, being thus, does not grieve after death.

503.

503.

“Akkodhanonupanāhī, amāyo rittapesuṇo;

Guttadvāro sadā bhikkhu, evaṃ pecca na socati.

“A bhikkhu who is not prone to anger, not resentful, free from deceit, and devoid of slander, who is always with guarded doors; being thus, he does not grieve after death.

504.

504.

“Akkodhanonupanāhī[M 0.0296][V 0.0233], amāyo rittapesuṇo;

Kalyāṇasīlo so yo (syā.) bhikkhu, evaṃ pecca na socati.

A bhikkhu who is not prone to anger, who is not resentful, who is free from deceit and devoid of slander, and is of virtuous conduct; practicing thus, he does not grieve after death.

505.

505.

“Akkodhanonupanāhī, amāyo rittapesuṇo;

Kalyāṇamitto so bhikkhu, evaṃ pecca na socati.

“A bhikkhu who is not prone to anger, not resentful, free from deceit, and devoid of slander, that bhikkhu with admirable friends; being thus, he does not grieve after death.

506.

506.

“Akkodhanonupanāhī[P 0.0053], amāyo rittapesuṇo;

Kalyāṇapañño so bhikkhu, evaṃ pecca na socati.

“A bhikkhu who is not prone to anger, not resentful, free from deceit, and devoid of slander, that bhikkhu of admirable wisdom; being thus, he does not grieve after death.

507.

507.

“Yassa saddhā tathāgate, acalā suppatiṭṭhitā;

Sīlañca [T 0.0343] yassa kalyāṇaṃ, ariyakantaṃ pasaṃsitaṃ.

“One whose faith in the Tathāgata is unshaken and well established, and whose virtue is admirable, pleasing to the noble ones, and praised;

508.

508.

“Saṅghe pasādo yassatthi, ujubhūtañca dassanaṃ;

‘Adaliddo’ti taṃ āhu, amoghaṃ tassa jīvitaṃ.

“One who has confidence in the Saṅgha and whose view has become upright—they call him one who is not poor; his life is not in vain.

509.

509.

“Tasmā saddhañca sīlañca, pasādaṃ dhammadassanaṃ;

Anuyuñjetha medhāvī, saraṃ buddhāna sāsana”nti.

“Therefore, a wise person should be devoted to faith and virtue, confidence and the vision of the Dhamma, remembering the teaching of the Buddhas.”

… Sirimitto thero….

Thus the Elder Sirimitta spoke these verses.

3. Mahāpanthakattheragāthā

3. The Verses of the Elder Mahāpanthaka

510.

510.

“Yadā paṭhamamaddakkhiṃ, satthāramakutobhayaṃ;

Tato me ahu saṃvego, passitvā purisuttamaṃ.

When for the first time I saw the Teacher, who is fearless from any quarter, a sense of spiritual urgency arose in me on seeing the supreme person.

511.

511.

“Siriṃ hatthehi pādehi, yo paṇāmeyya āgataṃ;

Etādisaṃ so satthāraṃ, ārādhetvā virādhaye.

One who would spurn with hands and feet the good fortune that has arrived—such a person, having won the favor of such a Teacher, might then lose it.

512.

512.

“Tadāhaṃ puttadārañca, dhanadhaññañca chaḍḍayiṃ;

Kesamassūni chedetvā, pabbajiṃ anagāriyaṃ.

Then I abandoned son and wife, wealth and grain; having cut off my hair and beard, I went forth into the homeless life.

513.

513.

“Sikkhāsājīvasampanno, indriyesu susaṃvuto;

Namassamāno sambuddhaṃ, vihāsiṃ aparājito.

Endowed with the training and a livelihood in common, well-restrained in the sense faculties, paying homage to the Perfectly Enlightened One, I dwelt undefeated.

514.

514.

“Tato me paṇidhī āsi, cetaso abhipatthito;

Na nisīde muhuttampi, taṇhāsalle anūhate.

Then this resolution, this aspiration of my mind, arose in me: ‘I will not sit down even for a moment while the dart of craving is unextracted.’

515.

515.

“Tassa mevaṃ viharato, passa vīriyaparakkamaṃ;

Tisso vijjā anuppattā, kataṃ buddhassa sāsanaṃ.

For me dwelling thus—behold my energy and striving! The three knowledges have been attained; the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.

516.

516.

“Pubbenivāsaṃ [M 0.0297] jānāmi, dibbacakkhu visodhitaṃ;

Arahā dakkhiṇeyyomhi, vippamutto nirūpadhi.

I know my former abodes, the divine eye has been purified; I am an Arahant, worthy of offerings, completely liberated, without attachments.

517.

517.

“Tato [T 0.0344][V 0.0234] ratyā vivasāne vivasane (sī. syā.), sūriyassuggamanaṃ pati;

Sabbaṃ taṇhaṃ visosetvā, pallaṅkena upāvisi”nti.

Then at the end of the night, toward the rising of the sun, having dried up all craving, I sat down cross-legged.

… Mahāpanthako thero….

… The Elder Mahāpanthaka …

Aṭṭhakanipāto niṭṭhito.

The Book of the Eights is finished.

Tatruddānaṃ –

The summary therein:

Mahākaccāyano thero, sirimitto mahāpanthako;

The Elder Mahākaccāyana, Sirimitta, Mahāpanthaka;

Ete aṭṭhanipātamhi, gāthāyo catuvīsatīti.

These are in the Book of the Eights; the verses are twenty-four.

9. Navakanipāto

9. The Book of the Nines

1. Bhūtattheragāthā

1. The Verses of the Elder Bhūta

518.

518.

“Yadā [M 0.0298][V 0.0235][P 0.0054] dukkhaṃ jarāmaraṇanti paṇḍito, aviddasū yattha sitā puthujjanā;

Dukkhaṃ pariññāya satova jhāyati, tato ratiṃ paramataraṃ na vindati.

When the wise one knows aging and death to be suffering—wherein ignorant worldlings are attached—having fully comprehended that suffering, he mindfully meditates; he finds no delight more excellent than that.

519.

519.

“Yadā dukkhassāvahaniṃ visattikaṃ, papañcasaṅghātadukhādhivāhiniṃ;

Taṇhaṃ pahantvāna satova jhāyati, tato ratiṃ paramataraṃ na vindati.

When, having abandoned that craving—which brings suffering, is an attachment, and leads to the affliction of the mass of proliferation—he mindfully meditates, he finds no delight more excellent than that.

520.

520.

“Yadā sivaṃ dvecaturaṅgagāminaṃ, magguttamaṃ [T 0.0345] sabbakilesasodhanaṃ;

Paññāya passitva satova jhāyati, tato ratiṃ paramataraṃ na vindati.

When, having seen with wisdom the peaceful, supreme path with its eight factors, which purifies all defilements, he mindfully meditates, he finds no delight more excellent than that.

521.

521.

“Yadā asokaṃ virajaṃ asaṅkhataṃ, santaṃ padaṃ sabbakilesasodhanaṃ;

Bhāveti saññojanabandhanacchidaṃ, tato ratiṃ paramataraṃ na vindati.

When one develops the sorrowless, dustless, unconditioned, peaceful state—the purification from all defilements, the cutting of the bonds of the fetters—one finds no delight more excellent than that.

522.

522.

“Yadā nabhe gajjati meghadundubhi, dhārākulā vihagapathe samantato;

Bhikkhū ca pabbhāragatova jhāyati, tato ratiṃ paramataraṃ na vindati.

When the cloud-drum thunders in the sky, and torrents of rain fill the birds’ path all around, and a monk, having gone to a mountain cave, meditates, he finds no delight more excellent than that.

523.

523.

“Yadā nadīnaṃ kusumākulānaṃ, vicitta-vāneyya-vaṭaṃsakānaṃ;

Tīre nisinno sumanova jhāyati, tato ratiṃ paramataraṃ na vindati.

When, sitting on the bank of rivers teeming with flowers, adorned with various forest blossoms as their crests, a monk of good mind meditates, he finds no delight more excellent than that.

524.

524.

“Yadā [M 0.0299] nisīthe rahitamhi kānane, deve gaḷantamhi nadanti dāṭhino;

Bhikkhū ca pabbhāragatova jhāyati, tato ratiṃ paramataraṃ na vindati.

When at midnight in a secluded forest, while the rain god pours and the tusked beasts roar, a monk, having gone to a mountain cave, meditates, he finds no delight more excellent than that.

525.

525.

“Yadā [T 0.0346] vitakke uparundhiyattano, nagantare nagavivaraṃ samassito;

Vītaddaro vītakhilova jhāyati, tato ratiṃ paramataraṃ na vindati.

When, having restrained his own thoughts, resorting to a mountain cleft or a mountain cave, free from anguish and free from mental barrenness, he meditates, he finds no delight more excellent than that.

526.

526.

“Yadā [P 0.0055] sukhī malakhilasokanāsano, niraggaḷo nibbanatho visallo;

Sabbāsave byantikatova jhāyati, tato ratiṃ paramataraṃ na vindatī”ti.

When, happy, a destroyer of stain, mental barrenness, and sorrow, unbolted, free from craving, dartless, having made an end of all the taints, he meditates, he finds no delight more excellent than that.

… Bhūto thero….

… The Elder Bhūta…

Navakanipāto niṭṭhito.

The Book of the Nines is finished.

Tatruddānaṃ –

The summary therein:

Bhūto tathaddaso thero, eko khaggavisāṇavā;

Navakamhi nipātamhi, gāthāyopi imā navāti.

The Elder Bhūta, who sees things as they are, alone like a rhinoceros; here in this Book of the Nines, there are these nine verses.

10. Dasakanipāto

10. The Book of the Tens

1. Kāḷudāyittheragāthā

1. The Verses of the Elder Kāḷudāyī

527.

527.

“Aṅgārino [M 0.0300][V 0.0236][P 0.0056] dāni dumā bhadante, phalesino chadanaṃ vippahāya;

Te accimantova pabhāsayanti, samayo mahāvīra bhāgī rasānaṃ.

Venerable sir, the trees are now like embers; having shed their foliage, they are aspiring to fruit. They blaze as if with flames. It is time, Great Hero, for the partaking of essences.

528.

528.

“Dumāni [T 0.0347] phullāni manoramāni, samantato sabbadisā pavanti;

Pattaṃ pahāya phalamāsasānā phalamāsamāno (ka.), kālo ito pakkamanāya vīra.

The trees are in full bloom and delightful; their fragrance spreads in all directions. Having shed their leaves and hoping for fruit, O Hero, it is time to depart from here.

529.

529.

“Nevātisītaṃ na panātiuṇhaṃ, sukhā utu addhaniyā bhadante;

Passantu taṃ sākiyā koḷiyā ca, pacchāmukhaṃ rohiniyaṃ tarantaṃ.

Venerable sir, it is neither too cold nor too hot; the season is pleasant for a long journey. May the Sākyans and the Koḷiyans see you crossing the Rohiṇī, facing westwards.

530.

530.

“Āsāya kasate khettaṃ, bījaṃ āsāya vappati;

Āsāya vāṇijā yanti, samuddaṃ dhanahārakā;

Yāya āsāya tiṭṭhāmi, sā me āsā samijjhatu.

With hope the farmer plows the field; with hope the seed is sown. With hope merchants, seekers of wealth, travel the sea. The hope for which I stand—may that hope of mine be fulfilled.

531.

531.

saṃ. ni. 1.198 “Punappunaṃ ceva vapanti bījaṃ, punappunaṃ vassati devarājā;

Punappunaṃ khettaṃ kasanti kassakā, punappunaṃ dhaññamupeti raṭṭhaṃ.

Again and again they sow the seed, again and again the king of the devas sends rain; again and again farmers plow the field, again and again grain comes to the kingdom.

532.

532.

saṃ. ni. 1.198 “Punappunaṃ yācanakā caranti, punappunaṃ dānapatī dadanti;

Punappunaṃ dānapatī daditvā, punappunaṃ saggamupenti ṭhānaṃ.

Again and again beggars wander about; again and again patrons give. Having given again and again, patrons again and again go to a heavenly place.

533.

533.

“Vīro [T 0.0348][P 0.0057] have sattayugaṃ puneti, yasmiṃ kule jāyati bhūripañño;

Maññāmahaṃ sakkati devadevo, tayā hi jāto tayābhijāto (sī.) muni saccanāmo.

A hero of vast wisdom indeed purifies seven generations in the clan in which he is born. I think that you, O God of gods, are able to purify even more; for you are the Sage, truly so-named, born of the noble path.

534.

534.

“Suddhodano [M 0.0301] nāma pitā mahesino, buddhassa mātā pana māyanāmā;

Yā bodhisattaṃ parihariya kucchinā, kāyassa bhedā tidivamhi modati.

Suddhodana by name was the father of the Great Seer, and the Buddha’s mother was named Māyā. She who carried the Bodhisatta in her womb, after the breaking up of the body, rejoices in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

535.

535.

“Sā gotamī kālakatā ito cutā, dibbehi kāmehi samaṅgibhūtā;

Sā modati kāmaguṇehi pañcahi, parivāritā devagaṇehi tehi.

That Gotamī, having passed away and departed from here, is endowed with divine sensual pleasures; she rejoices in the five strands of sensual pleasure, surrounded by those hosts of devas.

536.

536.

“Buddhassa puttomhi asayhasāhino, aṅgīrasassappaṭimassa tādino;

Pitupitā mayhaṃ tuvaṃsi sakka, dhammena me gotama ayyakosī”ti.

I am the son of the Buddha, the unassailable conqueror, of the Aṅgīrasa, the incomparable, the steadfast one. You, O Sākyan, are the father of my Father; by the Dhamma, O Gotama, you are my grandfather.

… Kāḷudāyī thero….

… The Elder Kāḷudāyī …

2. Ekavihāriyattheragāthā

2. The Verses of the Elder Ekavihāriya

537.

537.

“Purato [V 0.0237] pacchato vāpi, aparo ce na vijjati;

Atīva phāsu bhavati, ekassa vasato vane.

If before or behind no other is to be found, it is exceedingly pleasant for one dwelling alone in the forest.

538.

538.

“Handa [T 0.0349] eko gamissāmi, araññaṃ buddhavaṇṇitaṃ;

Phāsu phāsuṃ (syā. pī.) ekavihārissa, pahitattassa bhikkhuno.

Come, I will go alone to the forest praised by the Buddha; it is pleasant for a bhikkhu dwelling alone, who has directed his mind.

539.

539.

“Yogī-pītikaraṃ rammaṃ, mattakuñjarasevitaṃ;

Eko attavasī khippaṃ, pavisissāmi kānanaṃ.

Inspiring joy in the yogī, delightful, frequented by intoxicated elephants; alone, seeking my own welfare, I will quickly enter the woodland.

540.

540.

“Supupphite sītavane, sītale girikandare;

Gattāni parisiñcitvā, caṅkamissāmi ekako.

In the well-flowered, cool forest, in a cool mountain gorge, having bathed my limbs, I will practice walking meditation, solitary.

541.

541.

“Ekākiyo adutiyo, ramaṇīye mahāvane;

Kadāhaṃ viharissāmi, katakicco anāsavo.

Alone, without a second, in the delightful great forest, when shall I dwell, my task done, free from taints?

542.

542.

“Evaṃ me kattukāmassa, adhippāyo samijjhatu;

Sādhiyissāmahaṃyeva, nāñño aññassa kārako.

May this intention of mine, who wishes to act thus, succeed. I myself shall accomplish it; no one can act for another.

543.

543.

“Esa [M 0.0302] bandhāmi sannāhaṃ, pavisissāmi kānanaṃ;

Na tato nikkhamissāmi, appatto āsavakkhayaṃ.

Here I bind on my armor and will enter the woodland. I will not leave it until I have attained the destruction of the taints.

544.

544.

“Mālute upavāyante, sīte surabhigandhike gandhake (syā. pī. ka.);

Avijjaṃ dālayissāmi, nisinno nagamuddhani.

While the cool and fragrant breezes blow, I will shatter ignorance, seated on a mountain peak.

545.

545.

“Vane kusumasañchanne, pabbhāre nūna sītale;

Vimuttisukhena sukhito, ramissāmi giribbaje.

Indeed, in the forest covered with flowers, on a cool mountain slope, made happy by the bliss of liberation, I will delight in Giribbaja.

546.

546.

“Sohaṃ [P 0.0058] paripuṇṇasaṅkappo, cando pannaraso yathā;

Sabbāsavaparikkhīṇo, natthi dāni punabbhavo”ti.

With my intention fulfilled, like the full moon on the fifteenth day, with all taints destroyed, for me there is now no renewed existence.

… Ekavihāriyo thero….

Thus the Elder Ekavihāriya spoke these verses.

3. Mahākappinattheragāthā

3. The Verses of the Elder Mahākappina

547.

547.

“Anāgataṃ [T 0.0350] yo paṭikacca paṭigacca (sī.) passati, hitañca atthaṃ ahitañca taṃ dvayaṃ;

Viddesino tassa hitesino vā, randhaṃ na passanti samekkhamānā.

One who, reflecting, foresees what is to come—that pair, the beneficial and the harmful—his enemies or his well-wishers, though scrutinizing him, do not find a fault.

548.

548.

paṭi. ma. 1.160 paṭisambhidāmagge “Ānāpānasatī yassa, paripuṇṇā subhāvitā;

Anupubbaṃ paricitā, yathā buddhena desitā;

Somaṃ lokaṃ pabhāseti, abbhā muttova candimā.

One whose mindfulness of breathing is complete and well-developed, cultivated in sequence as taught by the Buddha, illuminates this world like the moon freed from a cloud.

549.

549.

“Odātaṃ [V 0.0238] vata me cittaṃ, appamāṇaṃ subhāvitaṃ;

Nibbiddhaṃ paggahītañca, sabbā obhāsate disā.

Oh, my mind is pure, immeasurable, and well-developed; penetrated and uplifted, it illuminates all directions.

550.

550.

“Jīvate vāpi sappañño, api vittaparikkhayo;

Paññāya ca alābhena, vittavāpi na jīvati.

A wise person lives on even when his wealth is destroyed; but through lack of wisdom, even a wealthy person does not truly live.

551.

551.

“Paññā sutavinicchinī, paññā kittisilokavaddhanī;

Paññāsahito naro idha, api dukkhesu sukhāni vindati.

Wisdom is the arbiter of what is heard; wisdom increases fame and renown. A person endowed with wisdom here finds happiness even amid suffering.

552.

552.

“Nāyaṃ ajjatano dhammo, nacchero napi abbhuto;

Yattha jāyetha mīyetha, tattha kiṃ viya abbhutaṃ.

This is no principle of today, nothing amazing or wonderful. That one dies where one was born—what is so wonderful in that?

553.

553.

“Anantaraṃ hi jātassa, jīvitā maraṇaṃ dhuvaṃ;

Jātā jātā marantīdha, evaṃdhammā hi pāṇino.

Indeed, for one who has been born, death is certain to follow life. All who are born here die; such is the nature of living beings.

554.

554.

“Na [M 0.0303] hetadatthāya matassa hoti, yaṃ jīvitatthaṃ paraporisānaṃ;

Matamhi ruṇṇaṃ na yaso na lokyaṃ, na [T 0.0351] vaṇṇitaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇehi.

Weeping is of no benefit to the dead. It brings no fame, no worldly gain, nor is it praised by ascetics and brahmins.

555.

555.

“Cakkhuṃ sarīraṃ upahanti tena upahanti ruṇṇaṃ (sī.), upahanti roṇṇaṃ (syā. pī.), nihīyati vaṇṇabalaṃ matī ca;

Ānandino tassa disā bhavanti, hitesino nāssa sukhī bhavanti.

By it one harms one's eyes and body; one's complexion, strength, and intelligence decline. His enemies rejoice over it, while his well-wishers are not made happy.

556.

556.

“Tasmā hi iccheyya kule vasante, medhāvino ceva bahussute ca;

Yesaṃ [P 0.0059] hi paññāvibhavena kiccaṃ, taranti nāvāya nadiṃva puṇṇa”nti.

Therefore, one should wish for wise and learned members to be dwelling in one's family. For by the power of their wisdom, people accomplish their tasks, like crossing a full river with a boat.

… Mahākappino thero….

… The Elder Mahākappina …

4. Cūḷapanthakattheragāthā

4. The Verses of the Elder Cūḷapanthaka

557.

557.

“Dandhā mayhaṃ gatī āsi, paribhūto pure ahaṃ;

Bhātā ca maṃ paṇāmesi, ‘gaccha dāni tuvaṃ gharaṃ’.

My understanding was slow; formerly I was despised. And my brother dismissed me, saying: ‘Now you go home.’

558.

558.

“Sohaṃ paṇāmito santo bhātā (aṭṭha.), saṅghārāmassa koṭṭhake;

Dummano tattha aṭṭhāsiṃ, sāsanasmiṃ apekkhavā.

Having been dismissed, I stood disheartened at the monastery’s gatehouse, still longing for the Dispensation.

559.

559.

“Bhagavā tattha āgacchi āgañchi (sī. pī.), sīsaṃ mayhaṃ parāmasi;

Bāhāya maṃ gahetvāna, saṅghārāmaṃ pavesayi.

The Blessed One came there and stroked my head; taking me by the arm, he led me into the monastery.

560.

560.

“Anukampāya me satthā, pādāsi pādapuñchaniṃ;

‘Etaṃ suddhaṃ adhiṭṭhehi, ekamantaṃ svadhiṭṭhitaṃ’.

Out of compassion for me, the Teacher gave a foot-wiping cloth, saying: ‘Resolve upon this clean object, well-established in a secluded place.’

561.

561.

“Tassāhaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā, vihāsiṃ sāsane rato;

Samādhiṃ [T 0.0352] paṭipādesiṃ, uttamatthassa pattiyā.

Having heard his word, I dwelled delighting in the Dispensation; I brought concentration to fulfillment for the attainment of the ultimate goal.

562.

562.

“Pubbenivāsaṃ [V 0.0239] jānāmi, dibbacakkhu visodhitaṃ;

Tisso vijjā anuppattā, kataṃ buddhassa sāsanaṃ.

I know my former abodes, the divine eye is purified; the three true knowledges have been attained, the Buddha’s teaching has been done.

563.

563.

“Sahassakkhattumattānaṃ[M 0.0304], nimminitvāna panthako;

Nisīdambavane ramme, yāva kālappavedanā.

Panthaka created himself a thousand times and sat in the delightful mango grove until the time was announced.

564.

564.

“Tato me satthā pāhesi, dūtaṃ kālappavedakaṃ;

Paveditamhi kālamhi, vehāsādupasaṅkamiṃ vehāsānupasaṅkamiṃ (syā. ka.).

Then the Teacher sent me a messenger to announce the time. When the time was announced, I approached through the air.

565.

565.

“Vanditvā satthuno pāde, ekamantaṃ nisīdahaṃ;

Nisinnaṃ maṃ viditvāna, atha satthā paṭiggahi.

Having paid homage at the Teacher’s feet, I sat down to one side. Knowing that I was seated, the Teacher then accepted the offering.

566.

566.

“Āyāgo sabbalokassa, āhutīnaṃ paṭiggaho;

Puññakkhettaṃ manussānaṃ, paṭigaṇhittha dakkhiṇa”nti.

Worthy of offerings from the whole world, a receiver of sacrificial gifts, a field of merit for humankind, he accepted the dedicated gift.

… Cūḷapanthako thero….

… The Elder Cūḷapanthaka …

5. Kappattheragāthā

5. The Verses of the Elder Kappa

567.

567.

“Nānākulamalasampuṇṇo, mahāukkārasambhavo;

Candanikaṃva paripakkaṃ, mahāgaṇḍo mahāvaṇo.

Filled with various kinds of filth, sprung from a great heap of refuse; like a ripe cesspit, a great boil, a great wound.

568.

568.

“Pubbaruhirasampuṇṇo, gūthakūpena gāḷhito gūthakūpe nigāḷhito (syā. pī. ka.);

Āpopaggharaṇo kāyo, sadā sandati pūtikaṃ.

Full of pus and blood, steeped in a pit of excrement; the body is a source of oozing, always trickling what is foul.

569.

569.

“Saṭṭhikaṇḍarasambandho[P 0.0060], maṃsalepanalepito;

Cammakañcukasannaddho, pūtikāyo niratthako.

Bound by sixty sinews, plastered with a coating of flesh, clad in a jacket of skin—a foul and worthless body.

570.

570.

“Aṭṭhisaṅghātaghaṭito, nhārusuttanibandhano;

Nekesaṃ saṃgatībhāvā, kappeti iriyāpathaṃ.

Constructed from a collection of bones, bound with threads of sinews; from the coming together of many parts, it produces its postures.

571.

571.

“Dhuvappayāto [T 0.0353] maraṇāya, maccurājassa santike;

Idheva chaḍḍayitvāna, yenakāmaṅgamo naro.

Headed for certain death, into the presence of the King of Death; having abandoned it right here, a person goes wherever he wishes.

572.

572.

“Avijjāya nivuto kāyo, catuganthena ganthito;

Oghasaṃsīdano kāyo, anusayajālamotthato.

A body veiled by ignorance, tied up with the four knots; a body sinking in the flood, overspread with the net of underlying tendencies.

573.

573.

“Pañcanīvaraṇe yutto, vitakkena samappito;

Taṇhāmūlenānugato, mohacchādanachādito.

Yoked to the five hindrances, afflicted by thought, pursued by the root of craving, covered by the cloak of delusion.

574.

574.

“Evāyaṃ vattate kāyo, kammayantena yantito;

Sampatti ca vipatyantā, nānābhāvo vipajjati.

Thus this body proceeds, impelled by the machine of kamma. Success has failure as its end; its diverse nature perishes.

575.

575.

“Yemaṃ [M 0.0305][V 0.0240] kāyaṃ mamāyanti, andhabālā puthujjanā;

Vaḍḍhenti kaṭasiṃ ghoraṃ, ādiyanti punabbhavaṃ.

Those blind, foolish worldlings who consider this body ‘mine’ enlarge the horrid charnel ground and take on renewed existence.

576.

576.

“Yemaṃ kāyaṃ vivajjenti, gūthalittaṃva pannagaṃ;

Bhavamūlaṃ vamitvāna, parinibbissantināsavā”ti parinibbantunāsavā (sī.).

But those who shun this body as one would a snake smeared with filth, having vomited up the root of being, will attain final Nibbāna without taints.”

… Kappo thero….

… The Elder Kappa …

6. Vaṅgantaputtaupasenattheragāthā

6. The Verses of the Elder Upasena, Son of Vaṅganta

577.

577.

“Vivittaṃ appanigghosaṃ, vāḷamiganisevitaṃ;

Seve senāsanaṃ bhikkhu, paṭisallānakāraṇā.

A bhikkhu should frequent a lodging that is secluded, quiet, frequented by beasts of prey, for the purpose of solitary meditation.

578.

578.

“Saṅkārapuñjā āhatvā āhitvā (ka.), susānā rathiyāhi ca;

Tato saṅghāṭikaṃ katvā, lūkhaṃ dhāreyya cīvaraṃ.

Having collected rags from rubbish heaps, from charnel grounds, and from streets, and having made a patchwork robe from them, a bhikkhu should wear that coarse robe.

579.

579.

“Nīcaṃ manaṃ karitvāna, sapadānaṃ kulā kulaṃ;

Piṇḍikāya care bhikkhu, guttadvāro susaṃvuto.

Having humbled his mind, a bhikkhu should walk for alms from family to family in sequence, with doors guarded, well-restrained.

580.

580.

“Lūkhenapi vā lūkhenapi ca (bahūsu) santusse, nāññaṃ patthe rasaṃ bahuṃ;

Rasesu [T 0.0354] anugiddhassa, jhāne na ramatī mano.

One should be content even with coarse food and not desire many other flavors. For one greedy for flavors, the mind does not delight in jhāna.

581.

581.

“Appiccho ceva santuṭṭho, pavivitto vase muni;

Asaṃsaṭṭho gahaṭṭhehi, anāgārehi cūbhayaṃ.

The sage should dwell with few wishes, contented, and secluded, unassociated with both householders and the homeless.

582.

582.

“Yathā jaḷo va mūgo va, attānaṃ dassaye tathā;

Nātivelaṃ sambhāseyya, saṅghamajjhamhi paṇḍito.

A wise one should show himself as if dull and mute; he should not speak at length in the midst of the Sangha.

583.

583.

“Na so upavade kañci, upaghātaṃ vivajjaye;

Saṃvuto pātimokkhasmiṃ, mattaññū cassa bhojane.

He should not disparage anyone; he should avoid doing harm. He should be restrained in the Pātimokkha and be moderate in eating.

584.

584.

“Suggahītanimittassa, cittassuppādakovido;

Samaṃ anuyuñjeyya, kālena ca vipassanaṃ.

Skilled in the arising of the mind, having well grasped the meditation sign, he should cultivate serenity and, at the proper time, insight.

585.

585.

“Vīriyasātaccasampanno[P 0.0061], yuttayogo sadā siyā;

Na ca appatvā dukkhantaṃ, vissāsaṃ eyya paṇḍito.

Endowed with energy and perseverance, he should always be devoted to the practice. A wise one should not become complacent before reaching the end of suffering.

586.

586.

“Evaṃ viharamānassa, suddhikāmassa bhikkhuno;

Khīyanti āsavā sabbe, nibbutiñcādhigacchatī”ti.

For a bhikkhu dwelling thus, one who desires purity, all the taints are destroyed, and he attains Nibbāna.”

… Upaseno vaṅgantaputto thero….

Thus the Elder Upasena, son of Vaṅganta, spoke these verses.

7. (Apara)-gotamattheragāthā

7. The Verses of Another Elder Gotama

587.

587.

“Vijāneyya [M 0.0306][V 0.0241] sakaṃ atthaṃ, avalokeyyātha pāvacanaṃ;

Yañcettha assa patirūpaṃ, sāmaññaṃ ajjhupagatassa.

One should discern one’s own good and examine the scriptures. One should also consider what is suitable therein for one who has undertaken the ascetic’s life.

588.

588.

“Mittaṃ idha ca kalyāṇaṃ, sikkhā vipulaṃ samādānaṃ;

Sussūsā ca garūnaṃ, etaṃ samaṇassa patirūpaṃ.

Good friends here, undertaking the extensive training, and eagerness to learn from one's teachers—this is befitting for a recluse.

589.

589.

“Buddhesu sagāravatā, dhamme apaciti yathābhūtaṃ;

Saṅghe [T 0.0355] ca cittikāro, etaṃ samaṇassa patirūpaṃ.

Reverence for the Buddhas, true respect for the Dhamma, and high esteem for the Sangha—this is befitting for a recluse.

590.

590.

“Ācāragocare yutto, ājīvo sodhito agārayho;

Cittassa ca saṇṭhapanaṃ, etaṃ samaṇassa patirūpaṃ.

Devoted to good conduct and resort, a purified and blameless livelihood, and the stabilizing of the mind—this is befitting for a recluse.

591.

591.

“Cārittaṃ atha vārittaṃ, iriyāpathiyaṃ pasādaniyaṃ;

Adhicitte ca āyogo, etaṃ samaṇassa patirūpaṃ.

Observances and avoidance, inspiring deportment, and application to the higher mind—this is befitting for a recluse.

592.

592.

“Āraññakāni senāsanāni, pantāni appasaddāni;

Bhajitabbāni muninā, etaṃ samaṇassa patirūpaṃ.

Wilderness lodgings, remote and quiet, should be frequented by the sage—this is befitting for a recluse.

593.

593.

“Sīlañca bāhusaccañca, dhammānaṃ pavicayo yathābhūtaṃ;

Saccānaṃ abhisamayo, etaṃ samaṇassa patirūpaṃ.

Virtue and great learning, true investigation of phenomena, and the penetration of the truths—this is befitting for a recluse.

594.

594.

“Bhāveyya ca aniccanti, anattasaññaṃ asubhasaññañca;

Lokamhi ca anabhiratiṃ, etaṃ samaṇassa patirūpaṃ.

One should cultivate the perception of impermanence, the perception of not-self, the perception of foulness, and non-delight in the world—this is befitting for a recluse.

595.

595.

“Bhāveyya ca bojjhaṅge, iddhipādāni indriyāni balāni;

Aṭṭhaṅgamaggamariyaṃ, etaṃ samaṇassa patirūpaṃ.

One should develop the factors of enlightenment, the bases of spiritual power, the faculties, the powers, and the Noble Eightfold Path—this is befitting for a recluse.

596.

596.

“Taṇhaṃ pajaheyya muni, samūlake āsave padāleyya;

Vihareyya vippamutto, etaṃ samaṇassa patirūpa”nti.

The sage should abandon craving, he should shatter the taints with their root, and dwell fully released—this is befitting for a recluse.”

… Gotamo thero….

… The Elder Gotama …

Dasakanipāto niṭṭhito.

The Book of the Tens is finished.

Tatruddānaṃ –

The summary:

Kāḷudāyī ca so thero, ekavihārī ca kappino;

Cūḷapanthako kappo ca, upaseno ca gotamo;

Sattime dasake therā, gāthāyo cettha sattatīti.

The Elder Kāḷudāyī, Ekavihārī, and Kappina, Cūḷapanthaka and Kappa, Upasena and Gotama: these seven elders are in the Book of the Tens, and herein are seventy verses.

11. Ekādasanipāto

11. The Book of Elevens

1. Saṃkiccattheragāthā

1. The Verses of the Elder Saṃkicca

597.

597.

“Kiṃ [T 0.0356][M 0.0307][V 0.0242][P 0.0062] tavattho vane tāta, ujjuhānova pāvuse;

Verambhā ramaṇīyā te, paviveko hi jhāyinaṃ.

What benefit is there for you, dear son, dwelling in the forest? And what benefit is the Ujjuhāna mountain for you in the rainy season? What is delightful for you in the Verambha winds? Truly, for those who meditate, seclusion is to be desired.”

598.

598.

“Yathā abbhāni verambho, vāto nudati pāvuse;

Saññā me abhikiranti, vivekapaṭisaññutā.

Just as the Verambha wind dispels the clouds in the rainy season, so too do my perceptions connected with seclusion pervade me.”

599.

599.

“Apaṇḍaro aṇḍasambhavo, sīvathikāya niketacāriko;

Uppādayateva me satiṃ, sandehasmiṃ virāganissitaṃ.

“A black crow, born from an egg, that frequents its home in the charnel ground—it indeed arouses in me a mindfulness based on dispassion for this body.”

600.

600.

“Yañca aññe na rakkhanti, yo ca aññe na rakkhati;

Sa ve bhikkhu sukhaṃ seti, kāmesu anapekkhavā.

“The monk whom others do not guard, and who does not guard others—that one indeed dwells happily, being without longing for sensual pleasures.”

601.

601.

“Acchodikā puthusilā, gonaṅgulamigāyutā;

Ambusevālasañchannā, te selā ramayanti maṃ.

“With clear water and broad slabs of rock, frequented by wild oxen, monkeys, and deer, covered with water-moss—those mountains delight me.”

602.

602.

“Vasitaṃ me araññesu, kandarāsu guhāsu ca;

Senāsanesu pantesu, vāḷamiganisevite.

“I have dwelt in forests, in ravines and in caves, in remote lodgings frequented by beasts of prey and deer.”

603.

603.

“‘Ime haññantu vajjhantu, dukkhaṃ pappontu pāṇino’;

Saṅkappaṃ nābhijānāmi, anariyaṃ dosasaṃhitaṃ.

“‘May these beings be struck, may they be killed, may they come to suffering!’—I do not recall ever having had such an ignoble thought connected with hatred.”

604.

604.

“Pariciṇṇo mayā satthā, kataṃ buddhassa sāsanaṃ;

Ohito garuko bhāro, bhavanetti samūhatā.

“The Teacher has been served by me, the Buddha’s teaching has been done; the heavy burden has been laid down, the conduit to existence has been uprooted.”

605.

605.

“Yassa catthāya yassatthāya (sī.) pabbajito, agārasmānagāriyaṃ;

So me attho anuppatto, sabbasaṃyojanakkhayo.

“The purpose for which I went forth from the home life into homelessness—that goal has been attained by me: the destruction of all fetters.”

606.

606.

“Nābhinandāmi [T 0.0357] maraṇaṃ, nābhinandāmi jīvitaṃ;

Kālañca paṭikaṅkhāmi, nibbisaṃ bhatako yathā.

“I do not delight in death, I do not delight in life; I await the time, just as a hired servant awaits his wage.”

607.

607.

“Nābhinandāmi [M 0.0308][V 0.0243] maraṇaṃ, nābhinandāmi jīvitaṃ;

Kālañca paṭikaṅkhāmi, sampajāno patissato”ti.

“I do not delight in death, I do not delight in life; I await the time, fully aware and mindful.”

… Saṃkicco thero….

Thus the Elder Saṃkicca spoke these verses.

Ekādasanipāto niṭṭhito.

The Chapter of Elevens is finished.

Tatruddānaṃ –

The summary there:

Saṃkiccathero ekova, katakicco anāsavo;

Ekādasanipātamhi, gāthā ekādaseva cāti.

The Elder Saṃkicca, the only one, his task done, taintless; in the Chapter of Elevens, the verses are indeed eleven.

12. Dvādasakanipāto

12. The Chapter of Twelves

1. Sīlavattheragāthā

1. The Verses of the Elder Sīlava

608.

608.

“Sīlamevidha [M 0.0309][V 0.0244][P 0.0063] sikkhetha, asmiṃ loke susikkhitaṃ;

Sīlaṃ hi sabbasampattiṃ, upanāmeti sevitaṃ.

“One should train only in virtue here in this world, being well-trained; for virtue, when cultivated, leads to all accomplishment.”

609.

609.

“Sīlaṃ rakkheyya medhāvī, patthayāno tayo sukhe;

Pasaṃsaṃ vittilābhañca, pecca sagge pamodanaṃ pecca sagge ca modanaṃ (sī. pī.).

“A wise person, aspiring for the three kinds of happiness, should guard virtue: praise and the acquisition of wealth, and, after passing away, rejoicing in heaven.”

610.

610.

“Sīlavā hi bahū mitte, saññamenādhigacchati;

Dussīlo pana mittehi, dhaṃsate pāpamācaraṃ.

“Indeed, a virtuous person gains many friends through self-restraint; but an immoral person, practicing evil, is deprived of friends.”

611.

611.

“Avaṇṇañca akittiñca, dussīlo labhate naro;

Vaṇṇaṃ kittiṃ pasaṃsañca, sadā labhati sīlavā.

“An immoral person gains dispraise and ill-repute; a virtuous person always gains praise, renown, and commendation.”

612.

612.

“Ādi [T 0.0358] sīlaṃ patiṭṭhā ca, kalyāṇānañca mātukaṃ;

Pamukhaṃ sabbadhammānaṃ, tasmā sīlaṃ visodhaye.

“Virtue is the beginning and the foundation, the mother of good qualities, and the foremost of all wholesome states. Therefore, one should purify virtue.”

613.

613.

“Velā ca saṃvaraṃ sīlaṃ saṃvaro sīlaṃ (sī.), saṃvarasīlaṃ (sī. aṭṭha.), cittassa abhihāsanaṃ;

Titthañca sabbabuddhānaṃ, tasmā sīlaṃ visodhaye.

“Virtue is a boundary and a restraint, a delight for the mind, and the ford for all the Buddhas. Therefore, one should purify virtue.”

614.

614.

“Sīlaṃ balaṃ appaṭimaṃ, sīlaṃ āvudhamuttamaṃ;

Sīlamābharaṇaṃ seṭṭhaṃ, sīlaṃ kavacamabbhutaṃ.

“Virtue is an incomparable power, virtue is the supreme weapon; virtue is the best adornment, virtue is a marvelous armor.”

615.

615.

“Sīlaṃ setu mahesakkho, sīlaṃ gandho anuttaro;

Sīlaṃ vilepanaṃ seṭṭhaṃ, yena vāti disodisaṃ.

“Virtue is a mighty bridge, virtue is the unsurpassed fragrance, virtue is the best unguent, by which it wafts to all directions.”

616.

616.

“Sīlaṃ sambalamevaggaṃ, sīlaṃ pātheyyamuttamaṃ;

Sīlaṃ seṭṭho ativāho, yena yāti disodisaṃ.

“Virtue is the foremost provision, virtue is the supreme travel-supply; virtue is the best guide, by which one travels to all directions.”

617.

617.

“Idheva nindaṃ labhati, peccāpāye ca dummano;

Sabbattha dummano bālo, sīlesu asamāhito.

“Right here he receives blame, and after death is miserable in a woeful state. Everywhere the fool, not established in virtue, is miserable.”

618.

618.

“Idheva kittiṃ labhati, pecca sagge ca summano;

Sabbattha sumano dhīro, sīlesu susamāhito.

“Right here he gains renown, and after death is happy in heaven. Everywhere the wise one, well-established in virtue, is happy.”

619.

619.

“Sīlameva [V 0.0245] idha aggaṃ, paññavā pana uttamo;

Manussesu ca devesu, sīlapaññāṇato jaya”nti.

“Here virtue is indeed foremost, but one with wisdom is supreme. Among humans and gods, they conquer through virtue and wisdom.”

… Sīlavo thero….

… The Elder Sīlava …

2. Sunītattheragāthā

2. The Verses of the Elder Sunīta

620.

620.

“Nīce [M 0.0310] kulamhi jātohaṃ, daliddo appabhojano;

Hīnakammaṃ hīnaṃ kammaṃ (syā.) mamaṃ āsi, ahosiṃ pupphachaḍḍako.

“I was born in a low family, poor and with little food. My work was lowly; I was a flower-sweeper.”

621.

621.

“Jigucchito [T 0.0359] manussānaṃ, paribhūto ca vambhito;

Nīcaṃ manaṃ karitvāna, vandissaṃ bahukaṃ janaṃ.

“Despised by people, scorned and reviled, having humbled my mind, I paid homage to many people.”

622.

622.

“Athaddasāsiṃ [P 0.0064] sambuddhaṃ, bhikkhusaṅghapurakkhataṃ;

Pavisantaṃ mahāvīraṃ, magadhānaṃ puruttamaṃ.

“Then I saw the Fully Enlightened One, escorted by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, the Great Hero, entering the best city of the Magadhans.”

623.

623.

“Nikkhipitvāna byābhaṅgiṃ, vandituṃ upasaṅkamiṃ;

Mameva anukampāya, aṭṭhāsi purisuttamo.

“Having put down my carrying pole, I approached to pay homage. Out of compassion for me alone, the Supreme Person stood still.”

624.

624.

“Vanditvā satthuno pāde, ekamantaṃ ṭhito tadā;

Pabbajjaṃ ahamāyāciṃ, sabbasattānamuttamaṃ.

“Having paid homage to the Teacher’s feet, standing to one side, I then requested the going forth from the one supreme among all beings.”

625.

625.

“Tato kāruṇiko satthā, sabbalokānukampako;

‘Ehi bhikkhū’ti maṃ āha, sā me āsūpasampadā.

“Then the compassionate Teacher, sympathizer with the whole world, said to me, ‘Come, bhikkhu!’ That was my higher ordination.”

626.

626.

“Sohaṃ eko araññasmiṃ, viharanto atandito;

Akāsiṃ satthuvacanaṃ, yathā maṃ ovadī jino.

“Dwelling alone in the forest, unwearied, I carried out the Teacher’s word, just as the Victor had instructed me.”

627.

627.

“Rattiyā paṭhamaṃ yāmaṃ, pubbajātimanussariṃ;

Rattiyā majjhimaṃ yāmaṃ, dibbacakkhuṃ visodhayiṃ dibbacakkhu visodhitaṃ (ka.);

Rattiyā pacchime yāme, tamokhandhaṃ padālayiṃ.

“In the first watch of the night, I recollected my former lives. In the middle watch of the night, I purified the divine eye. In the last watch of the night, I shattered the mass of darkness.”

628.

628.

“Tato ratyā vivasāne, sūriyassuggamanaṃ pati;

Indo brahmā ca āgantvā, maṃ namassiṃsu pañjalī.

“Then, at the end of the night, at sunrise, Indra and Brahmā came and, with hands folded in reverence, paid homage to me.”

629.

629.

“‘Namo te purisājañña, namo te purisuttama;

Yassa te āsavā khīṇā, dakkhiṇeyyosi mārisa’.

“‘Homage to you, O thoroughbred of men! Homage to you, O supreme man! You whose taints are destroyed—O venerable sir, you are worthy of offerings.’”

630.

630.

“Tato [T 0.0360] disvāna maṃ satthā, devasaṅghapurakkhataṃ;

Sitaṃ pātukaritvāna, imamatthaṃ abhāsatha.

“Then the Teacher, seeing me escorted by the host of gods, manifested a smile and spoke this meaning:”

631.

631.

su. ni. 660 suttanipātepi “‘Tapena [M 0.0311][V 0.0246] brahmacariyena, saṃyamena damena ca;

Etena brāhmaṇo hoti, etaṃ brāhmaṇamuttama’”nti.

‘By austerity, by the holy life, by restraint, and by self-control—by this one is a brahmin. This is called the supreme brahmin.’

… Sunīto thero….

… The Elder Sunīta …

Dvādasakanipāto niṭṭhito.

The Chapter of Twelves is finished.

Tatruddānaṃ –

The summary therein:

Sīlavā ca sunīto ca, therā dve te mahiddhikā;

Dvādasamhi nipātamhi, gāthāyo catuvīsatīti.

Sīlava and Sunīta, those two elders of great power; in the Chapter of Twelves, there are twenty-four verses.

13. Terasanipāto

13. The Chapter of Thirteens

1. Soṇakoḷivisattheragāthā

1. The Verses of the Elder Soṇa Koḷivisa

632.

632.

“Yāhu [M 0.0312][V 0.0247][P 0.0065] raṭṭhe samukkaṭṭho, rañño aṅgassa paddhagū patthagū (syā.), paṭṭhagū (ka.);

Svājja dhammesu ukkaṭṭho, soṇo dukkhassa pāragū.

He who was foremost in the realm, an attendant noble of the king of Aṅga, that Soṇa is today foremost in the Dhamma, one who has gone to the far shore of suffering.

633.

633.

“Pañca chinde pañca jahe, pañca cuttari bhāvaye;

Pañcasaṅgātigo bhikkhu, oghatiṇṇoti vuccati.

One should cut off five, abandon five, and further cultivate five. A bhikkhu who has overcome the five attachments is called ‘one who has crossed the flood’.

634.

634.

“Unnaḷassa pamattassa, bāhirāsassa bāhirāsayassa (ka.) bhikkhuno;

Sīlaṃ samādhi paññā ca, pāripūriṃ na gacchati.

For a bhikkhu who is arrogant, heedless, and whose aspiration is external, virtue, concentration, and wisdom do not come to fulfillment.

635.

635.

“Yañhi kiccaṃ apaviddhaṃ tadapaviddhaṃ (sī. syā.), akiccaṃ pana karīyati;

Unnaḷānaṃ [T 0.0361] pamattānaṃ, tesaṃ vaḍḍhanti āsavā.

For those by whom what should be done is neglected, while what should not be done is performed—for them, the arrogant and heedless, the taints increase.

636.

636.

“Yesañca susamāraddhā, niccaṃ kāyagatā sati;

Akiccaṃ te na sevanti, kicce sātaccakārino;

Satānaṃ sampajānānaṃ, atthaṃ gacchanti āsavā.

But for those by whom mindfulness directed to the body is ever well-aroused, they do not resort to what should not be done and are persistent in what should be done. For them, the mindful and clearly comprehending, the taints go to destruction.

637.

637.

“Ujumaggamhi akkhāte, gacchatha mā nivattatha;

Attanā codayattānaṃ, nibbānamabhihāraye.

The straight path has been proclaimed. Go, do not turn back! Urge yourself on by yourself; one should lead oneself to Nibbāna.

638.

638.

“Accāraddhamhi vīriyamhi, satthā loke anuttaro;

Vīṇopamaṃ karitvā me, dhammaṃ desesi cakkhumā;

Tassāhaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā, vihāsiṃ sāsane rato.

When my energy was over-exerted, the Teacher, unsurpassed in the world, the One with Vision, taught me the Dhamma, making the simile of the lute. Having heard his word, I dwelt delighting in the Dispensation.

639.

639.

“Samathaṃ paṭipādesiṃ, uttamatthassa pattiyā;

Tisso vijjā anuppattā, kataṃ buddhassa sāsanaṃ.

I established serenity for the attainment of the supreme goal. The three true knowledges have been attained; the Buddha’s teaching has been done.

640.

640.

“Nekkhamme nikkhame (ka.), nekkhammaṃ (mahāva. 244; a. ni. 6.55) adhimuttassa, pavivekañca cetaso;

Abyāpajjhādhimuttassa abyāpajjhādhimhattassa (ka.), upādānakkhayassa ca.

Of one intent on renunciation and on seclusion of mind, of one intent on non-ill will and on the destruction of clinging,

641.

641.

“Taṇhakkhayādhimuttassa, asammohañca cetaso;

Disvā āyatanuppādaṃ, sammā cittaṃ vimuccati.

Of one intent on the destruction of craving and on the non-delusion of mind, having seen the arising of the sense bases, the mind is rightly liberated.

642.

642.

“Tassa [P 0.0066] sammā vimuttassa, santacittassa bhikkhuno;

Katassa paṭicayo natthi, karaṇīyaṃ na vijjati.

For that bhikkhu, rightly liberated, with a peaceful mind, there is no accumulation of what has been done; there is nothing further to be done.

643.

643.

“Selo [M 0.0313][V 0.0248] yathā ekaghano ekaghano (ka.), vātena na samīrati;

Evaṃ rūpā rasā saddā, gandhā phassā ca kevalā.

Just as a solid, one-mass rock is not stirred by the wind, so too forms, tastes, sounds, odors, and all tactile objects,

644.

644.

“Iṭṭhā [T 0.0362] dhammā aniṭṭhā ca, nappavedhenti tādino;

Ṭhitaṃ cittaṃ visaññuttaṃ, vayañcassānupassatī”ti.

—both desirable and undesirable phenomena—do not make the Such-a-one tremble. His mind is steady and detached, and he observes their passing away.

… Soṇo koḷiviso thero….

… The Elder Soṇa Koḷivisa …

Terasanipāto niṭṭhito.

The Chapter of Thirteens is finished.

Tatruddānaṃ –

The summary:

Soṇo koḷiviso thero, ekoyeva mahiddhiko;

Terasamhi nipātamhi, gāthāyo cettha terasāti.

The Elder Soṇa Koḷivisa, the only one, of great spiritual power; in the Chapter of Thirteens, there are thirteen verses here.

14. Cuddasakanipāto

14. The Chapter of Fourteens

1. Khadiravaniyarevatattheragāthā

1. The Verses of the Elder Revata of the Acacia Forest

645.

645.

“Yadā [M 0.0314][V 0.0249][P 0.0067] ahaṃ pabbajito, agārasmānagāriyaṃ;

Nābhijānāmi saṅkappaṃ, anariyaṃ dosasaṃhitaṃ.

Ever since I went forth from the home life into homelessness, I am not aware of any ignoble intention associated with hatred.

646.

646.

“‘Ime haññantu vajjhantu, dukkhaṃ pappontu pāṇino’;

Saṅkappaṃ nābhijānāmi, imasmiṃ dīghamantare.

‘May these beings be struck! May they be slain! May they come to suffering!’—I am not aware of such an intention in this long interval.

647.

647.

“Mettañca abhijānāmi, appamāṇaṃ subhāvitaṃ;

Anupubbaṃ paricitaṃ, yathā buddhena desitaṃ.

But I am aware of loving-kindness, boundless and well-developed, gradually made familiar, as it was taught by the Buddha.

648.

648.

“Sabbamitto sabbasakho, sabbabhūtānukampako;

Mettacittañca mettaṃ cittaṃ (sī. syā.) bhāvemi, abyāpajjarato abyāpajjharato (sī. syā.) sadā.

A friend to all, a comrade to all, compassionate toward all beings, I develop a mind of loving-kindness, ever delighting in non-affliction.

649.

649.

“Asaṃhīraṃ asaṃkuppaṃ, cittaṃ āmodayāmahaṃ;

Brahmavihāraṃ bhāvemi, akāpurisasevitaṃ.

I gladden my mind, which is imperturbable and unshakable. I develop the divine abidings, not resorted to by base persons.

650.

650.

“Avitakkaṃ [T 0.0363] samāpanno, sammāsambuddhasāvako;

Ariyena tuṇhībhāvena, upeto hoti tāvade.

A disciple of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, having attained the state without thought-conception, is thereby endowed with the noble silence.

651.

651.

“Yathāpi pabbato selo, acalo suppatiṭṭhito;

Evaṃ mohakkhayā bhikkhu, pabbatova na vedhati.

Just as a rocky mountain, immovable and well-established, so too, through the destruction of delusion, a bhikkhu does not tremble, just like a mountain.

652.

652.

“Anaṅgaṇassa posassa, niccaṃ sucigavesino;

Vālaggamattaṃ pāpassa, abbhamattaṃva khāyati.

To a person without blemish, one who is ever seeking purity, an evil the size of a hair’s tip appears as large as a cloud.

653.

653.

“Nagaraṃ yathā paccantaṃ, guttaṃ santarabāhiraṃ;

Evaṃ gopetha attānaṃ, khaṇo vo mā upaccagā.

Just as a frontier city is guarded within and without, so should you guard yourself. Let not the opportune moment pass you by.

654.

654.

“Nābhinandāmi maraṇaṃ, nābhinandāmi jīvitaṃ;

Kālañca paṭikaṅkhāmi, nibbisaṃ bhatako yathā.

I do not delight in death, nor do I delight in life; I await the time, like a hireling awaiting his wages.

655.

655.

“Nābhinandāmi maraṇaṃ…pe… sampajāno patissato.

I do not delight in death… and so on… clearly comprehending and mindful.

656.

656.

“Pariciṇṇo mayā satthā, kataṃ buddhassa sāsanaṃ;

Ohito garuko bhāro, bhavanetti samūhatā.

The Teacher has been served by me, the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished. The heavy burden is laid down, the conduit to existence is uprooted.

657.

657.

“Yassa [M 0.0315][V 0.0250] catthāya pabbajito, agārasmānagāriyaṃ;

So me attho anuppatto, sabbasaṃyojanakkhayo.

The purpose for which I went forth from home into homelessness—that purpose has been attained by me: the destruction of all fetters.

658.

658.

“Sampādethappamādena, esā me anusāsanī;

Handāhaṃ parinibbissaṃ, vippamuttomhi sabbadhī”ti.

Strive on with heedfulness! This is my instruction. Now, I will attain Parinibbāna; I am liberated from everything.

… Khadiravaniyarevato thero….

… The Elder Revata of the Acacia Forest…

2. Godattattheragāthā

2. The Verses of the Elder Godatta

659.

659.

“Yathāpi bhaddo ājañño, dhure yutto dhurassaho dhurāsaho (aṭṭha.);

Mathito [T 0.0364] atibhārena, saṃyugaṃ nātivattati.

Just as a good thoroughbred bull, yoked to the shaft and able to bear the burden, though oppressed by a heavy load, does not abandon the yoke;

660.

660.

“Evaṃ paññāya ye tittā, samuddo vārinā yathā;

Na pare atimaññanti, ariyadhammova pāṇinaṃ.

So too, those who are replete with wisdom, as the ocean is with water, do not despise others; this is the very nature of the noble ones toward beings.

661.

661.

“Kāle [P 0.0068] kālavasaṃ pattā, bhavābhavavasaṃ gatā;

Narā dukkhaṃ nigacchanti, tedha socanti māṇavā mānavā (sī.).

In time, having fallen under the sway of time, having come under the sway of existence and non-existence, people arrive at suffering; those beings grieve here.

662.

662.

“Unnatā sukhadhammena, dukkhadhammena conatā;

Dvayena bālā haññanti, yathābhūtaṃ adassino.

Elated by conditions for happiness and dejected by conditions for suffering, fools who do not see things as they truly are, are afflicted by both.

663.

663.

“Ye ca dukkhe sukhasmiñca, majjhe sibbinimaccagū;

Ṭhitā te indakhīlova, na te unnataonatā.

But those who, in regard to pain, pleasure, and that in the middle, have overcome the seamstress, craving, they stand firm like an Indra's post, neither elated nor dejected.

664.

664.

“Na heva lābhe nālābhe, na yase na ca kittiyā;

Na nindāyaṃ pasaṃsāya, na te dukkhe sukhamhi.

Not in gain, nor in loss; not in disrepute, nor in fame; not in blame, nor in praise; not in pain, nor in pleasure are they shaken.

665.

665.

“Sabbattha te na limpanti, udabinduva pokkhare;

Sabbattha sukhitā dhīrā, sabbattha aparājitā.

In every way they are unsullied, like a drop of water on a lotus leaf. In every way the wise are happy, in every way they are unconquered.

666.

666.

“Dhammena ca alābho yo, yo ca lābho adhammiko;

Alābho dhammiko seyyo, yaṃ ce lābho adhammiko.

A non-gain that is righteous and a gain that is unrighteous: the righteous non-gain is better than the unrighteous gain.

667.

667.

“Yaso ca appabuddhīnaṃ, viññūnaṃ ayaso ca yo;

Ayasova seyyo viññūnaṃ, na yaso appabuddhinaṃ.

Fame from the unwise and disgrace from the wise: disgrace from the wise is better, not fame from the unwise.

668.

668.

“Dummedhehi [M 0.0316] pasaṃsā ca, viññūhi garahā ca yā;

Garahāva seyyo viññūhi, yaṃ ce bālappasaṃsanā.

Praise from the foolish and blame from the wise: blame from the wise is better than the praise of fools.

669.

669.

“Sukhañca [T 0.0365][V 0.0251] kāmamayikaṃ, dukkhañca pavivekiyaṃ;

Pavivekadukkhaṃ seyyo, yaṃ ce kāmamayaṃ sukhaṃ.

Sensual pleasure and the suffering of seclusion: the suffering of seclusion is better than sensual pleasure.

670.

670.

“Jīvitañca adhammena, dhammena maraṇañca yaṃ;

Maraṇaṃ dhammikaṃ seyyo, yaṃ ce jīve adhammikaṃ.

An unrighteous life and a righteous death: a righteous death is better than an unrighteous life.

671.

671.

“Kāmakopappahīnā ye, santacittā bhavābhave;

Caranti loke asitā, natthi tesaṃ piyāpiyaṃ.

Those who have abandoned sensual desire and anger, with minds at peace in every state of existence, wander in the world unattached; for them there is nothing dear or undear.

672.

672.

“Bhāvayitvāna bojjhaṅge, indriyāni balāni ca;

Pappuyya paramaṃ santiṃ, parinibbantināsavā”ti.

Having developed the enlightenment factors, the spiritual faculties, and the powers, having reached the supreme peace, the taintless ones attain final Nibbāna.

… Godatto thero….

Thus the Elder Godatta spoke these verses.

Cuddasakanipāto niṭṭhito.

The Chapter of Fourteens is finished.

Tatruddānaṃ –

The summary therein:

Revato ceva godatto, therā dve te mahiddhikā;

Cuddasamhi nipātamhi, gāthāyo aṭṭhavīsatīti.

Revata and Godatta, those two elders of great spiritual power; in the Chapter of Fourteens there are twenty-eight verses.

15. Soḷasakanipāto

15. The Book of the Sixteens

1. Aññāsikoṇḍaññattheragāthā

1. The Verses of the Elder Aññāsikoṇḍañña

673.

673.

“Esa [M 0.0317][V 0.0252][P 0.0069] bhiyyo pasīdāmi, sutvā dhammaṃ mahārasaṃ;

Virāgo desito dhammo, anupādāya sabbaso.

I am even more confident, having heard the Dhamma of great savor; the Dhamma taught is dispassion, for non-clinging in every way.

674.

674.

“Bahūni loke citrāni, asmiṃ pathavimaṇḍale;

Mathenti [T 0.0366] maññe saṅkappaṃ, subhaṃ rāgūpasaṃhitaṃ.

There are many diverse things in the world on this surface of the earth; they churn up, I think, beautiful thoughts connected with lust.

675.

675.

“Rajamuhatañca vātena, yathā meghopasammaye;

Evaṃ sammanti saṅkappā, yadā paññāya passati.

Just as dust raised up by the wind is settled by a rain cloud, so thoughts are stilled when one sees with wisdom.

676.

676.

dha. pa. 277 dhammapade “Sabbe saṅkhārā aniccāti, yadā paññāya passati;

Atha nibbindati dukkhe, esa maggo visuddhiyā.

“All conditioned things are impermanent”—when one sees this with wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with suffering: this is the path to purity.

677 .

677 .

dha. pa. 278 dhammapade “Sabbe saṅkhārā dukkhāti, yadā paññāya passati

Atha nibbindati dukkhe, esa maggo visuddhiyā.

“All conditioned things are suffering”—when one sees this with wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with suffering: this is the path to purity.

678.

678.

dha. pa. 279 dhammapade “Sabbe dhammā anattāti, yadā paññāya passati;

Atha nibbindati dukkhe, esa maggo visuddhiyā.

“All phenomena are non-self”—when one sees this with wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with suffering: this is the path to purity.

679.

679.

“Buddhānubuddho yo thero, koṇḍañño tibbanikkamo;

Pahīnajātimaraṇo, brahmacariyassa kevalī.

The elder Koṇḍañña, who awakened following the Buddha, was one of keen exertion; he has abandoned birth and death, and is one who has fulfilled the holy life in its entirety.

680.

680.

“Oghapāso daḷhakhilo daḷho khilo (syā. ka.), pabbato duppadālayo;

Chetvā khilañca pāsañca, selaṃ bhetvāna chetvāna (ka.) dubbhidaṃ;

Tiṇṇo pāraṅgato jhāyī, mutto so mārabandhanā.

The flood's snare, the firm stake, the mountain hard to shatter—having cut the stake and the snare, and having broken the impenetrable rock, the meditator has crossed over to the far shore, released from Māra’s bonds.

681.

681.

“Uddhato capalo bhikkhu, mitte āgamma pāpake;

Saṃsīdati mahoghasmiṃ, ūmiyā paṭikujjito.

A restless and fickle bhikkhu, by associating with bad friends, sinks into the great flood, overturned by a wave.

682.

682.

“Anuddhato acapalo, nipako saṃvutindriyo;

Kalyāṇamitto medhāvī, dukkhassantakaro siyā.

Not restless and not fickle, prudent, with senses restrained, having noble friends and being wise—such a one would make an end of suffering.

683.

683.

“Kālapabbaṅgasaṅkāso, kiso dhamanisanthato;

Mattaññū [T 0.0367] annapānasmiṃ, adīnamanaso naro.

Resembling a dark-jointed plant, lean, with veins prominent; moderate in food and drink, a man of undaunted mind.

684.

684.

“Phuṭṭho [V 0.0253] ḍaṃsehi makasehi, araññasmiṃ brahāvane;

Nāgo saṅgāmasīseva, sato tatrādhivāsaye.

Bitten by gadflies and mosquitoes in the forest, in the great wood, one should endure there mindfully, like a tusker at the head of a battle.

685.

685.

“Nābhinandāmi [M 0.0318] maraṇaṃ…pe… nibbisaṃ bhatako yathā.

I do not delight in death … as a hireling awaits his wages.

686.

686.

“Nābhinandāmi maraṇaṃ…pe… sampajāno patissato.

I do not delight in death … clearly comprehending and mindful.

687.

687.

“Pariciṇṇo mayā satthā…pe… bhavanetti samūhatā.

The Teacher has been served by me … the conduit to existence is uprooted.

688.

688.

“Yassa catthāya pabbajito, agārasmānagāriyaṃ;

So me attho anuppatto, kiṃ me saddhivihārinā”ti.

That purpose for which I went forth from home into homelessness—that purpose has been attained by me. What need have I of a co-resident?

… Aññāsikoṇḍañño aññākoṇḍañño (sī. syā.) thero….

Thus the Elder Aññāsikoṇḍañña spoke these verses.

2. Udāyittheragāthā

2. The Verses of the Elder Udāyī

689.

689.

a. ni. 6.43 “Manussabhūtaṃ sambuddhaṃ, attadantaṃ samāhitaṃ;

Iriyamānaṃ brahmapathe, cittassūpasame rataṃ.

The Perfectly Enlightened One, manifest as a human, self-tamed and composed, faring along the divine path, delighting in the calming of the mind.

690.

690.

“Yaṃ manussā namassanti, sabbadhammāna pāraguṃ;

Devāpi taṃ namassanti, iti me arahato sutaṃ.

He whom humans venerate, the one who has gone beyond all phenomena; even the devas venerate him—thus have I heard from the Arahant.

691.

691.

“Sabbasaṃyojanātītaṃ[P 0.0070], vanā nibbanamāgataṃ;

Kāmehi nekkhammarataṃ nikkhammarataṃ (ka.), muttaṃ selāva kañcanaṃ.

He has passed beyond all fetters, emerged from the jungle and attained Nibbāna; delighting in renunciation of sensual pleasures, he is released like gold from ore.

692.

692.

“Sa ve accaruci nāgo, himavāvaññe siluccaye;

Sabbesaṃ [T 0.0368] nāganāmānaṃ, saccanāmo anuttaro.

Indeed, that Nāga is of surpassing radiance, like the Himālaya among other rocky mountains. Among all who bear the name ‘nāga,’ his is the true name, the unsurpassed.

693.

693.

“Nāgaṃ vo kittayissāmi, na hi āguṃ karoti so;

Soraccaṃ avihiṃsā ca, pādā nāgassa te duve.

I will extol the Nāga to you, for he does no wrong. Gentleness and non-harming: these are the Nāga’s two feet.

694.

694.

“Sati ca sampajaññañca, caraṇā nāgassa tepare;

Saddhāhattho mahānāgo, upekkhāsetadantavā.

Mindfulness and clear comprehension are his other feet; the great Nāga has faith for his trunk, and equanimity for his white tusks.

695.

695.

“Sati gīvā siro paññā, vīmaṃsā dhammacintanā;

Dhammakucchisamāvāso, viveko tassa vāladhi.

Mindfulness is his neck, wisdom his head—investigation and reflection on the Dhamma. His belly is a harmonious abode of Dhamma, and seclusion is his tail.

696.

696.

“So jhāyī assāsarato, ajjhattaṃ susamāhito;

Gacchaṃ samāhito nāgo, ṭhito nāgo samāhito.

He is a meditator, delighting in tranquility, internally well composed. The Nāga is composed when walking; the Nāga is composed when standing.

697.

697.

“Sayaṃ samāhito nāgo, nisinnopi samāhito;

Sabbattha saṃvuto nāgo, esā nāgassa sampadā.

The Nāga is composed when lying down, and composed also when seated. The Nāga is restrained in every way: this is the Nāga’s accomplishment.

698.

698.

“Bhuñjati [M 0.0319] anavajjāni, sāvajjāni na bhuñjati;

Ghāsamacchādanaṃ laddhā, sannidhiṃ parivajjayaṃ.

He partakes of what is blameless and does not partake of what is blameworthy. Having obtained food and covering, he avoids storing them up.

699.

699.

“Saṃyojanaṃ [V 0.0254] aṇuṃ thūlaṃ, sabbaṃ chetvāna bandhanaṃ;

Yena yeneva gacchati, anapakkhova gacchati.

Having cut every fetter and bond, both subtle and gross, to whatever direction he goes, he goes without concern.

700.

700.

“Yathāpi udake jātaṃ, puṇḍarīkaṃ pavaḍḍhati;

Nopalippati toyena, sucigandhaṃ manoramaṃ.

Just as a white lotus, born and grown in the water, is unsullied by the water, fragrant and delightful;

701.

701.

“Tatheva ca loke jāto, buddho loke viharati;

Nopalippati lokena, toyena padumaṃ yathā.

Just so, born in the world, the Buddha dwells in the world, yet remains unsullied by the world, just as a lotus is unsullied by water.

702.

702.

“Mahāgini pajjalito, anāhāropasammati;

Aṅgāresu [T 0.0369] ca santesu, nibbutoti pavuccati.

A great fire, blazing, is stilled for lack of fuel; and when the embers are stilled, it is called ‘extinguished.’

703.

703.

“Atthassāyaṃ viññāpanī, upamā viññūhi desitā;

Viññissanti mahānāgā, nāgaṃ nāgena desitaṃ.

This simile, taught by the wise, is to make the meaning known. The great Nāgas will understand the Nāga described by a Nāga.

704.

704.

“Vītarāgo vītadoso, vītamoho anāsavo;

Sarīraṃ vijahaṃ nāgo, parinibbissatyanāsavo”ti.

Devoid of lust, hatred, and delusion, without taints, the Nāga, abandoning the body, will attain final Nibbāna, taintless.”

… Udāyī thero….

Thus the Elder Udāyī spoke these verses.

Soḷasakanipāto niṭṭhito.

The Chapter of the Sixteens is finished.

Tatruddānaṃ –

The summary therein:

Koṇḍañño ca udāyī ca, therā dve te mahiddhikā;

Soḷasamhi nipātamhi, gāthāyo dve ca tiṃsa cāti.

Koṇḍañña and Udāyī, those two elders of great psychic power; in the Chapter of the Sixteens there are thirty-two verses.

16. Vīsatinipāto

16. The Chapter of the Twenties

1. Adhimuttattheragāthā

1. The Verses of the Elder Adhimutta

705.

705.

“Yaññatthaṃ [M 0.0320][V 0.0255][P 0.0071] vā dhanatthaṃ vā, ye hanāma mayaṃ pure;

Avasesaṃ avase taṃ (sī. aṭṭha. mūlapāṭho), avasesānaṃ (aṭṭha.?) bhayaṃ hoti, vedhanti vilapanti ca.

“For the sake of sacrifice or for the sake of wealth, those whom we formerly killed—for the rest, fear arises; they tremble and they lament.

706.

706.

“Tassa te natthi bhītattaṃ, bhiyyo vaṇṇo pasīdati;

Kasmā na paridevesi, evarūpe mahabbhaye.

“But for you there is no state of fear; your complexion brightens all the more. Why do you not grieve in the face of such great fear?”

707.

707.

“Natthi cetasikaṃ dukkhaṃ, anapekkhassa gāmaṇi;

Atikkantā bhayā sabbe, khīṇasaṃyojanassa ve.

“There is no mental suffering, chieftain, for one who is without concern. All fears have indeed been transcended by one whose fetters are destroyed.

708.

708.

“Khīṇāya bhavanettiyā, diṭṭhe dhamme yathātathe;

Na [T 0.0370] bhayaṃ maraṇe hoti, bhāranikkhepane yathā.

“When the guide to existence is destroyed, and the Dhamma has been seen in this very life as it really is, there is no fear at death, just as when laying down a burden.

709.

709.

“Suciṇṇaṃ brahmacariyaṃ me, maggo cāpi subhāvito;

Maraṇe me bhayaṃ natthi, rogānamiva saṅkhaye.

“The holy life has been well-practiced by me, and the path has been well-developed. I have no fear of death, just as one has no fear of the destruction of diseases.

710.

710.

“Suciṇṇaṃ brahmacariyaṃ me, maggo cāpi subhāvito;

Nirassādā bhavā diṭṭhā, visaṃ pitvāva pītvāva (sī.) chaḍḍitaṃ.

“The holy life has been well-practiced by me, and the path has been well-developed. States of existence are seen as without gratification, like having drunk poison and vomited it.

711.

711.

“Pāragū anupādāno, katakicco anāsavo;

Tuṭṭho āyukkhayā hoti, mutto āghātanā yathā.

“One who has gone to the far shore, without clinging, his duty done, taintless, is content at the exhaustion of his life-span, like one freed from the execution block.

712.

712.

“Uttamaṃ dhammataṃ patto, sabbaloke anatthiko;

Ādittāva gharā mutto, maraṇasmiṃ na socati.

“Having attained the supreme nature of the Dhamma, needing nothing in the entire world, like one freed from a burning house, one does not grieve at death.

713.

713.

“Yadatthi saṅgataṃ kiñci, bhavo vā yattha labbhati;

Sabbaṃ anissaraṃ etaṃ, iti vuttaṃ mahesinā.

“Whatever conditioned thing exists, or wherever existence is found, all this is without a master—so it has been said by the Great Seer.

714.

714.

“Yo taṃ tathā pajānāti, yathā buddhena desitaṃ;

Na gaṇhāti bhavaṃ kiñci, sutattaṃva ayoguḷaṃ.

“One who understands this as it is, just as it was taught by the Buddha, does not grasp at any existence, just as one would not grasp a red-hot iron ball.

715.

715.

“Na me hoti ‘ahosi’nti, ‘bhavissa’nti na hoti me;

Saṅkhārā vigamissanti, tattha kā paridevanā.

“For me there is no ‘I was,’ nor is there for me ‘I will be.’ Formations will cease: what lamentation can there be in that?

716.

716.

“Suddhaṃ dhammasamuppādaṃ, suddhaṃ saṅkhārasantatiṃ;

Passantassa yathābhūtaṃ, na bhayaṃ hoti gāmaṇi.

“For one who sees as it really is the pure origination of phenomena and the pure continuity of formations, there is no fear, O chieftain.

717.

717.

“Tiṇakaṭṭhasamaṃ [M 0.0321][V 0.0256] lokaṃ, yadā paññāya passati;

Mamattaṃ so asaṃvindaṃ, ‘natthi me’ti na socati.

“When with wisdom one sees the world to be like grass and sticks, finding no ‘mineness’ there, one does not grieve with the thought, ‘There is nothing for me.’

718.

718.

“Ukkaṇṭhāmi [P 0.0072] sarīrena, bhavenamhi anatthiko;

Soyaṃ [T 0.0371] bhijjissati kāyo, añño ca na bhavissati.

“I am weary of this body; I have no need for existence. This very body will break up, and another will not come to be.

719.

719.

“Yaṃ vo kiccaṃ sarīrena, taṃ karotha yadicchatha;

Na me tappaccayā tattha, doso pemañca hehiti”.

“Whatever task you have with this body, do as you wish; on that account neither aversion nor affection will arise in me.”

720.

720.

Tassa taṃ vacanaṃ sutvā, abbhutaṃ lomahaṃsanaṃ;

Satthāni nikkhipitvāna, māṇavā etadabravuṃ.

Having heard his words, so amazing and hair-raising, the young men laid down their weapons and spoke thus:

721.

721.

“Kiṃ bhadante karitvāna, ko vā ācariyo tava;

Kassa sāsanamāgamma, labbhate taṃ asokatā”.

“Venerable sir, what have you done? Who is your teacher? By relying on whose teaching is this sorrowless state attained?”

722.

722.

“Sabbaññū sabbadassāvī, jino ācariyo mama;

Mahākāruṇiko satthā, sabbalokatikicchako.

“The All-knower, the All-seer, the Victor is my teacher; the greatly compassionate Teacher, the physician for the entire world.

723.

723.
